title: Why Are Some People Left-Handed?
hook: About 10% of humans favor their left hand — and the answer starts, surprisingly, in the spinal cord, not the brain.
key_points: About 10% of people are left-handed, and it isn't purely genetic — two left-handed parents have left-handed kids only 25-30% of the time, and identical twins agree just 20-30% of the time.
Genome studies have found around 40 gene variants linked to left-handedness, and most unexpectedly are tubulin genes, which build the microtubule scaffolding inside cells.

A study of 8-12-week-old fetuses found gene-expression differences between the left and right sides of the spinal cord — motor-circuit asymmetries that appear before the brain even wires up to the limbs.
Left-handers show more varied brain organization: 20-30% process language in the right hemisphere or both sides, versus the typical left-hemisphere dominance.
One evolutionary hypothesis ties right-hand dominance, which emerged roughly 2.8 million years ago in the genus Homo, to combat: heart placement makes left-handed strikes riskier for the attacker.
content_html: Roughly 1 in 10 people is left-handed, and despite being one of the most visible traits in biology, the question of why has been a stubborn mystery spanning genetics, embryology, and evolution.
extra_html: Handedness isn't simply inherited: two left-handed parents have left-handed children only 25-30% of the time, and identical twins — who share all their DNA — agree on handedness just 20-30% of the time. Genome-wide studies have turned up roughly 40 gene variants that nudge the odds toward left-handedness, and surprisingly, most of them are tubulin genes, which build the microtubule scaffolding inside cells — not genes anyone expected to matter for something this complex. The trait's origin appears to lie lower than the brain: a study of 8-to-12-week-old fetuses found strong gene-expression differences between the left and right sides of the spinal cord, creating motor-circuit asymmetries that show up before the brain has even wired itself to the limbs. Left-handers also show more varied brain organization overall, with 20-30% processing language in the right hemisphere or both sides, versus the typical left-hemisphere dominance. One evolutionary theory for why right-handedness became the majority default, emerging roughly 2.8 million years ago in the genus Homo, points to combat: because of where the heart sits, a left-handed strike exposes the attacker's own vulnerable side, so right-handers may have had a small survival edge that compounded over deep time.

related.hook: When you touch something hot, your hand jerks back before you even feel the pain — because the signal takes a shortcut through your spinal cord, skipping the brain.

related.hook: Every time a cell copies its DNA, tiny typos can slip in — most do nothing at all, a few cause disease, and rare ones fuel evolution.

flashcards.back_html: No — two left-handed parents produce left-handed children only 25-30% of the time, and identical twins agree on handedness just 20-30% of the time, so genetics alone doesn't determine it.

flashcards.prompt: What was surprising about the ~40 gene variants linked to left-handedness?

choices.text: Most are tubulin genes, which build microtubule scaffolding inside cells
They are the same genes known to cause color blindness
None of them are active before birth

flashcards.explanation_html: Researchers didn't expect a gene family that builds cellular scaffolding to turn out to matter for something as complex as hand preference.

flashcards.prompt: Where does handedness appear to originate developmentally, and what's the evidence?
flashcards.back_html: In the spinal cord, not the brain — a study found strong gene-expression differences between the left and right sides of the spinal cord in 8-to-12-week-old fetuses, before brain-to-limb connections even form.

flashcards.prompt: What's one evolutionary hypothesis for why right-handedness became the human majority?

choices.text: The "modified fighting hypothesis": heart placement makes left-handed strikes riskier for the attacker, giving right-handers a small survival edge
Right-handed people historically had more children for unrelated cultural reasons
Left-handedness only appeared after the invention of writing systems

flashcards.explanation_html: Because the heart sits slightly left, a left-handed strike exposes the attacker's own vulnerable side — a small edge that may have compounded over deep time since right-hand dominance emerged roughly 2.8 million years ago.
